notes: Would longer training help? LSTM with past weather, seed 0, NSE as the mean of 1 to 3 days ahead: stopped where the validation years say (update 125) training 0.33, validation 0.14, test 0.28; trained for a fixed 600 updates training 0.45, validation -0.12, test 0.17. The training score rises while the validation score falls: with only 20 years of one basin the model starts to memorise its training years (overfitting) almost at once, so early stopping halts it while it has learned little. These fixed-length runs are a diagnostic, not a model choice; the reported model is the validation-chosen one.

With the perfect weather forecast (wf, wqf) only the 3-days-ahead comparison with the baselines is like-for-like: the LSTM reads the weather of all three coming days at every lead, the baselines of 02_baselines.py only up to the target day. Weather stamped after the target day still tells about that day in this record: in the training years the river's day-to-day rise is correlated with the rain stamped on the same day (0.49) and on the next day (0.33), not two days later (0.00). So 1 and 2 days ahead the LSTM knows more than the baselines. Test NSE of the LSTM minus the best baseline, 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead: +0.08 / +0.09 / +0.00 (wf) and +0.06 / +0.09 / -0.01 (wqf). No winner is called for 1 and 2 days ahead with these two input sets (like_for_like is false in comparison.<set>.verdict).

Everything was chosen on the validation years 2000-2005 (stopping point, settings); the test years 2005-2014 were only scored. Test NSE in the tuning table and in hparam_log.csv is for the record and was not used.

Validation on one basin is fragile: 51% of the validation-year flow variance sits in 3 days (against 13% in the training and 15% in the test years). The two largest are the September 2004 hurricane floods: up to 200 mm of rain in one day (training-year maximum 153 mm), with the river peaking on the day of the rain. No model without a weather forecast can foresee that, so the validation NSE of this basin cannot be high and depends on a handful of days. Column val_nse_mean_before_2004_floods in hparam_log.csv scores the validation years up to one week before the larger flood (a drier stretch with less variance, so its level is not comparable); it is a diagnostic and was not used to choose anything.
train_nse_mean in hparam_log.csv is scored on the training years the model was fitted to (without the first days that have no forecast); it is there to show overfitting, not skill.

Tuning used one seed per value. The noise level is the spread of validation NSE over 3 seeds at the base setting (0.016); differences smaller than that are not real. Within the noise the smaller value was taken for model size and history, and the base value was kept for learning rate and dropout.
The chosen values were tuned one at a time and combined afterwards; the combination was checked against the base setting on validation years (see tuning.combination_check).

The setting was tuned with the river gauge as an input (wq) and used unchanged for the three other input sets. Chosen values at the edge of the range that was tried: model size 16, learning rate 0.005, history read before the first forecast 30; the best setting may lie outside the ranges tried.

Budget per run: at most 800 updates in tuning (half for hidden 128) and 2000 for the final models, validation check every 25 updates, stop after 6 checks without improvement. One update reads 32 stretches of one year, i.e. more than the whole 20 training years of this basin, so checks are closer together than for the all-basin model. This departs from the brief (a patience of about 4 checks, at the engine's default of 100 updates between checks): without a weather forecast the validation score of this basin peaks between update 50 and 350 and falls afterwards (tuning.base_curve), so checks 100 updates apart would step over the peak.
'History' (warmup) is the minimum number of days read before a scored forecast; within a block of 365 scored days later forecasts have read up to 365 days more.
w and wq: 3 seeds each, the saved prediction set is their day-by-day average. wf and wqf (perfect weather forecast, an upper bound that cannot be had in practice): one seed, no spread known.

Memory test: the model was trained with at least 30 days of history, so shorter contexts are outside what it was trained on; the test shows how much of the skill needs old weather, not how a model trained on short windows would do. Contexts above 395 days are longer than any stretch the model read in training.

Only the four knobs named in the plan were tuned. Batch size (32 one-year stretches per update) and the length of the scored stretch were left at the engine defaults; smaller batches might suit a single basin better and were not tried.
High flow = above the 95th percentile of the training years; onset = forecasts issued while the river was still at or below that level.
In the verdicts the LSTM is set against the like-for-like baseline with the highest test NSE at each lead, so it has to beat all of them; nothing was tuned or selected with that.

Training seconds (finals.*.seeds.*.training, hparam_log.csv) are wall-clock times on a laptop that smoke tests of other scripts shared at times: a rough cost measure only. updates_run, best_update and n_params are exact.
